title: KQL for Threat Hunting
monthTitle: Cloud SIEM & SOAR Operations with Microsoft Sentinel
summary: KQL (Kusto Query Language) is the language every Sentinel detection, hunt, and workbook is built on, so fluency here pays off everywhere else in the module. This lesson builds your skills from a single filter up to a real multi-table hunting query, covering the operators that do ninety percent of the work: where, project, extend, summarize ... by, count, sort/top, join, union, and let. You will master datetime math with ago() and bin(), the difference between has and contains, parsing fields out of messy strings, and arg_max() for getting the latest record per entity. Throughout you work against the real tables a SOC hunts in every day: SigninLogs, AuditLogs, SecurityEvent, DeviceProcessEvents, and DeviceNetworkEvents. By the end you can write runnable hunting queries that find failed sign-in bursts, rare process executions, and suspicious account activity.
objectives: Filter and shape data with where, project, and extend
Aggregate with summarize, count(), dcount(), and the by clause, bucketing time with bin()
Order and trim results using sort, top, and take
Combine tables with join and stack sources with union
Use let to parameterize hunts and arg_max() to get the latest record per entity
Apply ago() and datetime math, parse, and the has vs contains distinction in real hunting queries

quiz.q: Why is `has` usually preferred over `contains` when filtering a string column in KQL?
options: has is case-sensitive and contains is not
has matches whole indexed terms and is faster, while contains does a slower substring scan
contains cannot be used inside a where clause
has automatically deduplicates the result set
quiz.why: has matches on whole terms using the column's term index, so it is much faster on large tables. contains does an unindexed substring match anywhere in the value, which is slower and can produce noisy partial matches. Use contains only when you genuinely need a substring that is not a whole term.

quiz.q: What does `summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), IPAddress` produce?
options: A single total count for the whole table
One row per IP with its most recent event time
A count of events grouped into one-hour time buckets per IP address
The raw events sorted by time and IP
quiz.why: bin() rounds TimeGenerated down to the start of each one-hour window, and summarize ... by groups on that bucket plus IPAddress, so you get a count of events per IP per hour. This time-bucketing is the standard way to build trends and spot bursts.

quiz.q: You need the single most recent sign-in record for each user, keeping all that record's columns. Which is correct?
options: summarize max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName
summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by UserPrincipalName
top 1 by TimeGenerated
distinct UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated
quiz.why: arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) returns the row with the maximum TimeGenerated for each group and the * keeps every column from that winning row. max() alone returns only the timestamp, losing the rest of the record; top 1 limits the whole result, not per user.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between `union` and `join` in KQL?
options: union stacks rows from multiple tables together; join matches rows across tables on a shared key
union matches rows on a key; join stacks rows vertically
They are identical aliases for the same operation
union only works on numeric columns; join only on strings
quiz.why: union appends the rows of two or more tables into one result (vertical stacking), useful for combining similar event streams. join correlates rows from two tables horizontally where a key matches (for example linking a sign-in to a device event by account), letting you enrich or pivot across sources.

quiz.q: Why use `let` at the top of a hunting query?
options: It is required before any summarize statement
It permanently stores results in a new Sentinel table
It defines reusable variables or sub-results, making the query readable and easy to tune
It converts the query into an analytics rule automatically
quiz.why: let binds a value, list, or even a tabular sub-query to a name. You can set a lookback window, a threshold, or a list of known-bad IPs once at the top and reuse it, which makes hunts self-documenting and lets you tune one number instead of editing the body in several places.

quiz.q: Write, in plain English plus a short KQL sketch, how you would hunt for accounts experiencing a brute-force pattern of failed sign-ins from a single IP in the last 24 hours, and name two fields you would group or threshold on.
quiz.answer: Start from SigninLogs over the last 24 hours and keep only failures, where ResultType != 0 (or the non-zero error codes). Then summarize a count and a distinct count of targeted accounts per source IP and per hour, for example summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h). Finally filter for IPs that exceed a threshold, such as where Failures > 50 and Accounts > 5, which indicates one IP spraying many accounts rather than a single user mistyping a password. The fields I group and threshold on are IPAddress (the source) and the count of failures plus the distinct count of UserPrincipalName (the spread across accounts).
quiz.why: A real brute-force or password-spray hunt filters SigninLogs to failures, aggregates by source IP and time, and thresholds on both volume and the number of distinct accounts targeted, distinguishing an attack from ordinary user error.

resources.label: Hunt for threats with Microsoft Sentinel

body_markdown:
## Why KQL Is the Core Skill

Every analytics rule, every hunt, every workbook tile, and most automation triggers in Microsoft Sentinel are **KQL queries** underneath. If you can write KQL, you can detect, investigate, and report; if you can't, you are stuck clicking other people's content. KQL is a **read-only pipeline language**: you start with a table and pipe (`|`) it through operators that filter, reshape, aggregate, and join. Data flows left to right, top to bottom, and each operator transforms the rows coming into it.

The good news: about eight operators do ninety percent of real hunting. We'll build them up from a single filter to a full multi-table hunt.

## Filter and Shape: where, project, extend

Start by **filtering early** with `where` — it cuts the data the rest of the pipeline must process. `project` selects (and renames) only the columns you want; `extend` adds a new calculated column.

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0          // 0 means success; non-zero is a failure
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType, AppDisplayName
| extend FailureHour = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
```

Note `ago(24h)` — KQL has first-class **datetime math**. `ago(7d)`, `now()`, and arithmetic like `TimeGenerated > ago(1h)` are everywhere. Always put a time filter first; it is the cheapest, highest-impact filter you can apply.

## Aggregate: summarize, count, by, bin

`summarize` is the workhorse. It collapses many rows into grouped aggregates using functions like `count()`, `dcount()` (distinct count), `sum()`, `min()`, and `max()`, grouped by the columns after `by`. Bucketing time with `bin()` turns raw events into trends.

```kusto
// Failed sign-ins per source IP per hour over the last day
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
    by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| sort by Failures desc
```

This already looks like a detection: failures grouped by source IP and hour, plus how many distinct accounts each IP hit. An IP with high `Failures` **and** high `Accounts` is password-spraying.

## Order and Trim: sort, top, take

`sort by ... desc` orders results; `top N by Col` returns the N highest rows (a sort plus a limit); `take N` grabs an arbitrary N rows for a quick peek (not ordered, useful only for sampling).

```kusto
// The 10 noisiest source IPs by failed sign-ins
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize Failures = count() by IPAddress
| top 10 by Failures desc
```

## Find the Rare: summarize + thresholds

Threat hunting is often about **finding the rare**, not the common. On endpoints, a process that has only ever run a handful of times can be far more interesting than the busiest one. Group, count, then filter on the count.

```kusto
// Rarely-seen process executions in the last 7 days
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| summarize Executions = count(),
            Devices = dcount(DeviceName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by FileName, FolderPath
| where Executions <= 3 and Devices <= 2
| sort by Executions asc
```

Processes that ran only a couple of times on only a couple of devices are exactly where novel attacker tooling hides.

## Combine Sources: union and join

`union` **stacks** rows from similar tables; `join` **correlates** rows across tables on a shared key.

```kusto
// union: combine interactive and non-interactive sign-in failures
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize Failures = count() by UserPrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

```kusto
// join: which accounts that failed sign-in also spawned suspicious processes?
let failedAuth =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where ResultType != 0
    | distinct UserPrincipalName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe")
| join kind=inner (failedAuth) on $left.AccountUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName
| project TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, DeviceName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
```

The `kind=inner` keeps only rows that match on both sides. Other kinds (`leftouter`, `leftanti`) let you find rows that are present in one table but missing in another — `leftanti` is great for "first time we've ever seen this."

## let, parse, has vs contains, and arg_max

Four finishing skills tie real hunts together.

**`let`** binds reusable values or sub-queries at the top, so you tune one number instead of many:

```kusto
let lookback = 24h;
let failThreshold = 50;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
| where Failures > failThreshold and Accounts > 5
```

**`has` vs `contains`:** `has` matches whole indexed **terms** and is fast; `contains` does a slow substring scan. Prefer `has`.

```kusto
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID == 4688                    // a new process was created
| where CommandLine has "Invoke-WebRequest" // term match, fast
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine
```

**`parse`** pulls structured fields out of messy strings:

```kusto
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RemoteUrl has "login"
| parse RemoteUrl with "https://" Host "/" *
| summarize Connections = count() by Host, DeviceName
| sort by Connections desc
```

**`arg_max`** returns the full record with the maximum value per group — the standard way to get the **latest** state per entity:

```kusto
// Latest sign-in per user, keeping all columns of that record
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by UserPrincipalName
| project UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, IPAddress, Location, ResultType
```

## Putting It Together: a Real Hunt

Here is a complete, runnable hunt that finds source IPs spraying many accounts and enriches each with the account it most recently succeeded against — the kind of query you'd save as a Sentinel hunting query and later promote to an analytics rule.

```kusto
let lookback = 24h;
let sprayIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType != 0
    | summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where Failures > 50 and Accounts > 5;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType == 0                       // successful sign-ins
| join kind=inner (sprayIPs) on IPAddress
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, Location) by IPAddress, Failures, Accounts
| project IPAddress, Failures, Accounts, CompromisedHint = UserPrincipalName, Location, TimeGenerated
| sort by Failures desc
```

That single query filters, aggregates, thresholds, joins, and takes the latest record per group — every core operator working together. You are now ready to turn hunts like this into scheduled analytics rules.

slides.title: KQL for Threat Hunting
slides.sub: From a single filter to a real multi-table hunt
slides.narration: KQL is the language behind every Sentinel detection, hunt, and workbook, so this is the most leverage-rich lesson in the module. We'll build your fluency from one simple filter all the way up to a complete hunting query that finds password-spray attacks. Along the way you'll learn the eight operators that do ninety percent of real work, plus the time math, parsing, and arg_max tricks that make hunts practical against the tables a SOC lives in every day.

slides.title: KQL Is a Pipeline Language
bullets: Start with a table, pipe it through operators with the | symbol
Data flows left to right, top to bottom; each operator transforms rows
About eight operators cover most real hunting
Always filter early with a time bound to cut data volume
slides.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType
slides.narration: KQL is a read-only pipeline language. You begin with a table and pipe it through operators that filter, reshape, and aggregate, with data flowing top to bottom. The single most important habit is to filter early, especially on time with ago, because that cuts how much data the rest of the pipeline has to touch. Here we take the sign-in logs for the last day, keep only failures, and project just the columns we care about.

slides.title: Shape Data: where, project, extend
bullets: where filters rows; put the cheapest, most selective filters first
project selects and renames only the columns you need
extend adds a calculated column
ago() and datetime math are first-class in KQL
slides.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0
| extend FailureHour = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
slides.narration: Three operators shape your data. where filters rows, and you want your most selective filters first. project trims to just the columns you need, which keeps results readable and queries fast. extend adds a new computed column, here a one-hour bucket we'll use for trending. Notice ago of twenty-four hours: KQL treats datetimes as first-class, so time filters and arithmetic are everywhere in hunting.

slides.title: Aggregate: summarize, count, by, bin
bullets: summarize collapses rows into grouped aggregates
count(), dcount(), sum(), min(), max() are the common functions
by chooses the grouping columns
bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) buckets events into time windows for trends
slides.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize Failures = count(), Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
    by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| sort by Failures desc
slides.narration: summarize is the workhorse of hunting. It collapses many rows into aggregates like count and distinct count, grouped by whatever follows the by clause. Bucketing time with bin turns raw events into trends. This query already resembles a detection: failed sign-ins grouped by source IP and hour, plus how many distinct accounts each IP touched. An IP with both high failures and many accounts is password-spraying.

slides.title: Find the Rare, Not the Common
bullets: Hunting often means surfacing the rare, not the noisiest
Group, count, then filter on a low count threshold
Track FirstSeen and LastSeen with min/max of TimeGenerated
Novel attacker tooling hides in low-frequency executions
slides.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| summarize Executions = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceName)
    by FileName, FolderPath
| where Executions <= 3 and Devices <= 2
| sort by Executions asc
slides.narration: A lot of hunting is about finding the rare rather than the common. A process that has only ever run two or three times across one or two devices is far more suspicious than the busiest binary on the network. The pattern is simple: group, count, then filter on a small count. We also capture first-seen and last-seen with min and max of the timestamp. This is exactly where novel attacker tooling tends to hide.

slides.title: Combine Sources: union and join
bullets: union stacks rows from similar tables vertically
join correlates rows across tables on a shared key
kind=inner keeps only matches; leftanti finds what's missing
join identity failures to endpoint process events to pivot
slides.code:
let failedAuth =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | where ResultType != 0
    | distinct UserPrincipalName;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe")
| join kind=inner (failedAuth) on $left.AccountUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName
slides.narration: Two operators combine data. union stacks rows from similar tables, like merging interactive and non-interactive sign-ins. join correlates rows across different tables on a key, letting you pivot from identity to endpoint, for instance which accounts that failed sign-in also launched PowerShell. kind=inner keeps only matching rows, while leftanti is perfect for finding things present in one table but absent in another, the classic first-time-seen hunt.

slides.title: let, has vs contains, parse, arg_max
bullets: let binds reusable thresholds and sub-queries; tune one number
has matches whole indexed terms and is fast; contains is a slow substring scan
parse extracts structured fields out of messy strings
arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) returns the latest full record per entity
slides.code:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by UserPrincipalName
| project UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, IPAddress, Location, ResultType
slides.narration: Four finishing skills make hunts practical. let binds reusable values and sub-queries at the top, so you tune one threshold instead of many. Prefer has over contains: has matches whole indexed terms and is fast, while contains scans substrings slowly. parse pulls structured fields out of raw strings like URLs. And arg_max with a star returns the entire most-recent record per entity, the standard way to get each user's latest sign-in state.

slides.title: Putting It Together: a Real Hunt
bullets: Identify spray IPs: many failures across many accounts
Join back to successful sign-ins from those same IPs
arg_max surfaces the likely compromised account per IP
This hunt is one step from becoming an analytics rule
slides.code:
let sprayIPs =
    SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | where ResultType != 0
    | summarize Failures=count(), Accounts=dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where Failures > 50 and Accounts > 5;
SigninLogs
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=inner (sprayIPs) on IPAddress
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress, Failures, Accounts
slides.narration: Here every operator works together. First we isolate spray IPs with many failures spread across many accounts. Then we join back to successful sign-ins from those same IPs, because a success after a spray is the dangerous signal. arg_max surfaces the most recent account each IP got into. This single query filters, aggregates, thresholds, joins, and takes the latest record per group, and it is just one step away from becoming the scheduled analytics rule we build in the next lesson.
